text: A quantum chip's error rates are not a fixed spec printed on a datasheet — they're a snapshot of a system that keeps changing underneath you. This lesson covers why qubits drift, what providers do about it, and why it remains a real, ongoing operational burden.

It's natural to assume that once a qubit is built and characterized, its properties stay put. They don't. Three real physical sources cause measurable drift on timescales from minutes to days. Thermal fluctuations: even inside a dilution refrigerator near 10 to 20 millikelvin, small temperature changes shift some parameters measurably. Material defects: microscopic imperfections in the chip's dielectrics can behave like tiny two-level quantum systems that couple to the qubit and shift over time. And flux noise: for flux-tunable qubit designs, low-frequency magnetic noise causes the operating frequency to wander. None of these are design mistakes — they're intrinsic to the materials and environment involved.

Because of this drift, providers run periodic recalibration jobs — automated routines that re-measure key parameters and re-tune control pulses accordingly. A typical pass re-measures each qubit's resonant frequency, re-optimizes pulse amplitudes and timings, re-checks readout discrimination, and updates the published error-rate numbers. These routines run on a schedule set by the provider, and they're themselves a meaningful operational cost — time spent recalibrating is time the device isn't running user circuits.

Here's the key practical consequence: when a device page shows a two-qubit gate error of roughly one percent, that number reflects the most recent calibration run, not a permanent constant. By the time you submit a job, actual performance could be better or meaningfully worse, depending on how much drift has occurred since. It would be easy to describe recalibration as a solved background process — it isn't, fully. It takes machine time, it can't outrun drift faster than its own cadence, and it doesn't eliminate run-to-run variability, only bounds it. Anyone building a serious workload on real hardware should plan for drift as an ongoing fact of the platform.
Next lesson is the hands-on version: what's actually in the calibration data a provider publishes, and how a practitioner reads it to make a real decision.
